title: RUN!
reviewNotes: Three branches, 41 exact positions from a complete seven-piece root and separately reviewed later diagram. Root has c3/c4/d6/h6, not a b-pawn. First king walk ends ...Kxc3; omitted return walk remains context. With c3 gone, h8=Q defends a1 and ...Rxh8 gives c7 a tempo; second run allows connected seventh-rank pawns. h7 ...Rf8 draws, selected d7 then loses.
transcript: Fools would resign. Wise players might make a draw, [music] but only a true genius would be able to find the incredible win that white has in this position. You see, black is the only one with a rook left, but the white pawns are pretty close to promoting. But if white tries to be hasty and simply push the pawns, now after rook f8, the black [music] rook is going to be able to stop both of the pawns. It is going to be enough for black to walk in with the king, and the pawns are simply too slow. Black is going to be able to stop them and win the game. So, the first very precise move that [music] white needs to find is c5, sacrificing the pawn to the rook. But of course, if the pawn is taken, now we're going to be able to push. The rook cannot run to [music] the back rank, so it has to give this check and come around, but now we have gained a precious move with our king, and we are actually going to be able to bring him around to help the pawns and win this game. So, after c5, black tries to play king g3, now blocking the white king on the back rank, making sure that it can never run to help his subjects. Now, white has gained a precious tempo to start pushing the pawns. After h7, black has to run back to the back rank, and now hold back the pawns. Now, pushing the d-pawn wouldn't accomplish much. Remember, our king cannot come to the help of the pawns. So, white needs to play c6, trying to get the pawns to help each other down the board. But this is where things get interesting, because black can play rook to a8, now creating a checkmate threat. And it seems like black has at the very least secured a draw here. White has no other choice but to try and delay the checkmate threat with king to f1. Now, of course, this check would allow the king to escape, but of course, black can recreate the checkmate threat with king to f3. [music] And now the two kings engage in this dance. White tries to escape the death of the checkmate, [music] and black keeps recreating the threat. Until eventually, we reach to this position where the black king picks up the c-pawn. And now I want you to think about this. Whenever something changes in a position, even just a pawn disappearing, you need to reconsider and reassess the position. And that is exactly what white does in this position, because he starts to run all the way back to where he came from with his king. And now, once the kings reach [music] G1 and G3, because there is no C pawn anymore, we can now promote to a queen. And all the way from H8, this queen is making sure that the black rook cannot checkmate on A1. But of course, black can simply pick up this queen. But the reason why we ran back to this corner before promoting to the queen is the fact that the rook now is not actually threatening a checkmate. And so, we have one precious tempo to play C7. Black has nothing better but to recreate the checkmate threat. But now the two kings will dance again until eventually the white king runs to B1. >> [music] >> And without the black rook being able to give a check here, black cannot create the checkmate threat anymore. And so, we're going to get the other pawn one step away from promoting. And now there's going [music] to be no way to stop the promotion to a queen. If you love incredible chess, follow for more.
